utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. As the Chamber decided and indicated last week already, we are sitting with two judges pursuant to Rule 15 bis. The next witness should be brought in, please. And for the purpose of getting in the witness, we go for a short moment into closed session. Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we are now in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we turn back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please be patient. We wait for a moment so that the screens are opened. Good afternoon, sir, again. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card, the solemn declaration which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. The protective measures are still in place for you. That means the use of a pseudonym, nobody will address you with your real name in the courtroom, and your face will not be visible on the broadcast. Mr. McCloskey has questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Witness, good, you're getting your glasses on. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you know, we have some protective measures in place. Could we bring up 65 ter 6670 and, of course, not broadcast this so it's not seen. And has that come up on the screen, sir, and is your name in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. That is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we offer that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. Please wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P01447 under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, did you testify in the case of the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and the Prosecutor versus Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to listen to your testimony in those two cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And aside from some corrections that I think you made on the record in the last case, was everything true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked those same questions again that you were asked in those cases, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so, at this time, Mr. President, I would offer into evidence 65 ter 666 and 667, the Popovic transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you missed one 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Four 6s in the first one, and 6667 in the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, the first under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will wait patiently for the numbers to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first, which is 65 ter 666 -- 6666 shall be given Exhibit P01448. And the second, which is 65 ter 6667, shall be given Exhibit P01449, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the first one, which is 65 ter 6666, shall be admitted as Exhibit P01446 under seal, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you misspoke. It must be P1448 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we are on numbers, let me just finish that up. The Blagojevic testimony from 2003 is 65 ter number 1622. And if we could get a number for that, then I'll list the exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask what is the reason for tendering both transcripts? The transcripts in both cases? Is that really necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was a 92 bis witness for Popovic, so he wasn't asked very many questions and we basically relied on his testimony in Blagojevic, so that's -- with all these trials, I think that gives you -- not a repetitive situation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P014450, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the exhibits as listed on the associated exhibits that were admitted through this witness in the prior proceedings, I would offer all of those in and I will try to go through those numbers as we have them: 6668, 1166, 1167, 1168, 1174, 1176, 1343, 1345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received but we will give exhibit numbers, P numbers, by a memo from the Registrar. It's the most practical way, because of the amount of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I will read a summary, and I'm not going to ask you very many questions after that summary, but I will -- so listen to the summary, and if I've made any mistakes or errors, please let me know. The first paragraph of the summary I think it would be a good idea, Mr. President, if we could go in closed session for that. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The witness is a Bosnian Muslim. He was 17 years old in July 1995. Prior to the war, he lived with his family in the village of Nova Kasaba. After the occupation of nearby Cerska and Konjevic Polje, his family moved to the area around Srebrenica. We can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn back to public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From about the beginning of July 1995, there was shelling every day in the area around Srebrenica where the witness lived, and on 11 July, the witness, his father, his mother, and three sisters decided they had to leave their home as it was no longer safe to be there. They set off together to the village of Suceska, where they split up. The witness and his father went through the woods to the village of Jaglici and his mother and sisters went to the UN base in Potocari. On the 11th of July, in the afternoon, about 10.000 to 15.000 people, mostly men but including some young males and some women, gathered in this area around Jaglici and Susnjari. The witness heard at the time that there had been an order from the BiH army command that the men gather in that area. The witness was not in the BiH army at the time, but his father was. A column of people was formed. During the organisation of the column, the witness got separated from his father, whom he has not seen since. The witness found his uncle, and on the morning of the 12th of July, set off with him in the column. There were armed soldiers, BiH soldiers, at the front of the column, and some armed BiH soldiers at the back of the column. The witness was positioned towards the end of the column with the majority of civilians. The shelling began when the column entered the woods and continued throughout the day and into the night. General chaos had broken out and there were increasingly more injured people who were crying for help. He estimates he saw about 300 to 500 dead people in the woods. At about 10 a.m. on the 13th, Serb soldiers spoke over loudspeakers and said that the Muslims should surrender and that they would be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. The Serb soldiers threatened to kill anyone who did not surrender. Some people started surrendering, some committed suicide, some argued with each other, and others fled. The witness walked down to an asphalt road where he saw five or six soldiers telling people to surrender and to give up their belongings. Soon thereafter, Serb soldiers started to mistreat the people after they had surrendered. They cursed at them and asked for and took their money. As the group was taken to a meadow, the witness saw a dead body in civilian clothes and buses containing Muslim women and children. The witness estimates that there were about 1.000 to 2.000 Muslims present at the meadow, which was located not far from the village of Kravica. While at the meadow, the group was asked to repeat slogans like, "Long live Serbia, long live the king." Later that evening, a soldier at the meadow told everyone they would be taken to hangars in Bratunac and exchanged. Some of those who were born in 1980 or after were permitted to leave. The witness and others were then instructed to lay on their stomachs with their hands behind their necks. After about three hours, several large trucks arrived from the direction of Konjevic Polje and the witness and others were loaded onto them. It was hot inside, people were so jammed together they could not sit down. At around dusk, the truck drove to Bratunac and parked there overnight. The witness and the others remained on the truck in unbearable conditions. On the morning of the 14th, the truck set off and stopped just outside Bratunac where the witness and others were given a small amount of water. People on the witness's truck said they saw an UNPROFOR APC, but the witness did not see it. After approximately two hours, the trucks moved in the direction of Konjevic Polje and then towards Zvornik and Karakaj. After Karakaj, the trucks took a left and stopped at a building a while later. After about one hour, the witness and the others were taken off the truck and were directed to walk down the steps and into the building. Soldiers were standing on both sides of the steps, hitting and cursing at the people as they walked by. Once inside, the group was ordered up some stairs and told to repeat various chants or songs as they were taken up. At the top of the stairs, they turned left and were taken to a classroom. The witness recognised that he was in a school building at this point. The witness heard noises of people coming from the other classrooms. The witness estimated that there were approximately 200 people in the cramped classroom he was in. They were given a small amount of water, but everyone remained very thirsty. It was very stuffy, and when someone tried to open a window, shots were fired, breaking windows and wounding five or six men. The soldiers who were guarding them also threatened to kill two young men because of the noise that the group was making. While in the classroom, the witness heard beating and moaning coming from the hallway. Men were taken out of his classroom and they never returned. At about midnight, someone said the people in the classroom -- a Serb soldier said that the people in the classroom would be going out for an examination of some kind and exchanged. At that time, the witness and the others were led from the classroom and ordered to remove their shoes and shirts. After having their hands tied behind their backs, the people ordered down the stairs and onto a truck. The witness could feel something sticky on his feet as he walked by dead people in the front of the school. The truck the witness was in drove to a location about ten minutes away. When the truck stopped, the witness heard bursts of fire next to the truck. One man in his truck tried to run away and was shot. When the victim got off the truck, he was told by the Serb soldiers there to find a spot and lie down among the rows of people, all of whom were dead. As the witness fell forward, shots were fired and he felt pain at his elbow and the right side of his chest. The witness stayed still on the ground as the firing continued around him. He was hit with something in the foot. The soldier called out that anyone who was still warm will get a bullet in his head. A man lying next to the witness was then shot in the head at close range. Eventually, the soldiers left and the witness and another survivor were able to partially untie each other and escape the area just as another truck was approaching. The witness and his companion hid in a concrete canal or ditch while the killing continued. At daybreak, the witness and his companion discovered that there was a dam above the plateau where the killing had occurred. They also saw a loader that was picking up dead bodies. The witness and his companion wandered for several days before they made it to Muslim territory. The witness's uncle did not survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, witness, was that a correct summary of your experiences on those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: There is only at the beginning, when we arrived in Susnjari and Jaglici, you said that I wasn't a soldier at the time, but, in fact, I was -- I have never been a soldier. I was never a soldier either before or after or ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One moment. Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to ask you a couple of questions. You have testified many times that you left or were taken from that school building about midnight. Can you tell us how long the drive was from the school building to the execution site, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Around midnight we were taken out of the school building and loaded -- we actually climbed onto the truck. There were some boards placed there so we could walk up, and people kept on filling the truck. And the ride took about ten minutes to the place where they started taking us out of the trucks and killing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us roughly the space that the people that you saw that were dead took up, or any kind of rough estimate you can give us for when you got off the truck, what did you see, in terms of your dead friends and relatives and fellow Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: We were trying not to get off the truck. Nobody wanted to get out of the truck. One among us was trying to hide behind everybody, trying to prolong his life for a few minutes, but then you had to come out, everybody had to come out, so I did that as well, when I couldn't hide anymore, and when I jumped in front, to the left of the truck -- actually, to the right side of the truck, as we came off the truck, we went to the other side, they told us to find a place. I didn't know what they were talking about. When we got a little closer, you could see the lines of dead people. I don't know, it's difficult to make an estimate at a time like that, but perhaps some 20 metres, as far as you could see in the dark, it was night. The other person who survived, he was some two or three lines in front of me and there were other people to the left and to the right of him. Later, when I was crawling, I was crawling for a very long time until I left this plateau, until I could get into the trench, the ditch. In any case, there were more people there than the number of people who got off the truck. There was probably killing and wounding before. The next day as well. When we looked from the -- down the hill, a large area of the plateau was covered with the dead, and the loader was loading them into some kind of transport vehicle to be driven away somewhere. I really cannot tell how many there were. The truck was coming after as well, after we escaped. When we passed through the dead, when we got down into the ditch, another truck arrived, the shooting continued, the banging on the truck, but it was of a lesser intensity than before. Perhaps it was the last truck, because our classroom was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How far did your uncle make it with you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: He was in the classroom with me, and when we were ordered to leave, to come out two by two into the corridor, I asked him, "Are we going to go out together?" He said that we were not going to come out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you received information about your uncle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. I came out first and he stayed behind. But recently I was called because they had found him in one of the mass graves. The body wasn't whole. They called me to make the identification. They found him at the grave in Liplje, and this is a settlement between Zvornik and Konjevic Polje. It's quite far from this place. They told me what clothing he had, and it was the pair of trousers that he was wearing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about the fate of your father, who you were separated from on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. He was identified too. He was in the Nova Kasaba mass grave. With all his clothes. I went to identify the clothes. He was wearing all the clothes that he had on him when I lost him. He had been shot in the head. He was probably executed. And I know where he's buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have any cousins that you lost from those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My two cousins who lived in the same refugee settlement there. One lived in the same house with us and the other one didn't. When we were going in the direction of Suceska and when I went to Susnjari, they decided to go to Potocari. One has the same name as my father, except that he's older than my father. They were never soldiers. They went to Potocari. One was found in Pilica and the other one was found in another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us your father's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Alija Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the uncle's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Dzemal Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your cousins'?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Alija Avdic, just like my father, except he was older, and Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for coming for the -- I can't even count how many times it is now. You know better than I do, perhaps. Thank you very much. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much as well. Sir, whenever you need a break during the examination, please tell us and we will break. Now Mr. Tolimir has the right to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like for peace to reign in this house and I would like today's day and these proceedings to end as God wills it and not as I will it. I would like the witness to have a comfortable stay, and I wish peace in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are emotional after these questions because Mr. McCloskey put a series of questions to you. I'm not going to put questions like that to you because you answered in detail. I'm going to ask you about something that happened before these events and that is required in order to clarify some circumstances relevant to this trial. I would be very grateful if you could give some answers to these questions. During the examination-in-chief, line 14 -- actually, in your summary, after line 24, in line 24 on page 4 you said that you had gone to Jaglici with your father and that your mother and your sister went to Potocari. Do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you and your father and your mother and your sister agreed about the way how you could survive that situation in which you found yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Actually, it's not one sister. I had three sisters. My father told me to decide if I wanted to go to Potocari or to go with him. I felt that I should go with him, through the woods, in view of all the events in the war and before. I thought I could try to save myself, because my fears were justified, keeping in mind all my cousins who had gone to Potocari, including my neighbours who stayed behind in the settlement for the refugees or those who went to Potocari. They all died. So my fears were justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Since you decided to go, you have just described how you decided. Did you and your father give your mother and your sister some suggestions? I apologise, I said sister but you say you have -- you had three sisters. Did you give them some kind of suggestions, advice, instructions? Did you deliberately make the decision to separate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I don't remember that we gave any suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did others also separate, men and -- able-bodied men from other men and from women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: There was no rule. Those who wanted to could go to Potocari. Those who felt they would survive, they could go to Potocari. Those who didn't, they could go through the woods. Some could stay -- some stayed behind, and they are no longer among us. A man and a woman stayed behind in the settlement and their bones were found recently, all charred. There wasn't really that much difference, but people could choose where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, just to make it clear, it was everybody's personal decision. But let us now go back to the period before you set off that night. In line 21 to 23 of your testimony -- can we show to the witness his statement 65 ter 6624. Can we look at page 3 of your statement so that the witness could see what I'm asking him about. This is a statement -- let me say it for the transcript -- that you provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast because it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let it stay under seal. I'm going to put questions on the basis of it. I didn't want to speak out loud all the geographic information and things that would help to identify the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm looking at your statement now. We can all see it. I'm looking at the 21st, 22nd, and the 23rd row -- line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Can you start reading a sentence? It's very hard for me to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to read the sentence to you: "That is when we heard that members of our army or, actually, that the Chetniks were turned back to their starting positions, and soon after that you could hear explosions and we could hear the Muslim village near Srebrenica." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's very closely typed. It says, "We heard there ..." It is line 21.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the word in line 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Line 21, the sentence begins --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Just tell me the words, the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "We heard here that members of our army turned the Chetniks back to their starting positions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I really cannot find my way around. Perhaps somebody can show me where you are. Just tell me one word. You don't have to show me the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have been looking at the wrong page. We needed page 3. Now, this is page 3. Now I'm going to indicate with the cursor that you can see on your left-hand side what sentence that is. We need to go to the next page in the English as well. Lines 21, 22, 23. I'm going to mark those lines. "We heard there that members of our army --" Can we show the lines 21, 22, and 23 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be easier if you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you just start reading the relevant sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's start from line 20. You said, "That is where we were for one day." And then the sentence begins at 22: "We heard there that members of our army returned the Chetniks to their starting positions and soon after that that ours had withdrawn, that our people -- soldiers were returned to their starting positions." This is how the words end on 23.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I really cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You cannot see it, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: You will have to show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I will show it to you. Now perhaps we can see it in the e-court. I'm not able to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It also should be in the English e-court page 2. It's the wrong page there. And in English, if you look down the left and start with the word "Suceska" you can find the part he's talking about in English, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This version in the English, which I can understand, talks about the school, when we came to the school. Perhaps it's the correct page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now that we see the page in the e-court, now the marker is marking, the cursor is marking it. "We were there ..." You can see it. "That's where we heard ..." And it's in English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, let me read a few sentences before that in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's not necessary. The important thing is for you to see that: "That's where we were for one day. We spent a day there. Then we first heard that members of our army had pushed the Chetniks back to their initial positions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to know the line in the English version. Thank you very much. "We spent a day there," yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's the same line; 20, 21, 22, and 23 in English as well. It's very closely typed, so it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of what you read, my question is: When did you arrive at Vijogor? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but I think that it was the 10th or the 11th. I cannot remember the date right now. As we were leaving, after Slapovici, we spent one or two nights in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps you can redact these places so that it's not broadcast, what the witness said. So you were in Miokovo [phoen] for one night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you heard that your army had returned or retreated to their starting, to their initial positions. And before that they had pushed back the Serbian army back to their positions, but then they lost those positions. Can you please tell me, who did you hear this from? Were these rumours? Was this information that was confirmed and checked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: There were many people there. Women, children, lots of people. I heard it from someone. I don't know who I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to line 29, seven lines down from this sentence, where it says: "In the morning, we heard from the soldiers that NATO aeroplanes were expected to bomb the Serbian army."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: We heard it in the morning from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right. "... that NATO aeroplanes were expected to bomb the Serbian army and tanks. And that our forces were planning, if this should happen, to execute a counteraction in order to retake the lost positions." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we heard. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. Are you able to tell us, who did you hear this from about the expected NATO bombing and that your army would then retake their positions? Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, we heard it from someone. I don't know -- I don't remember who we heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could this information have been a product of somebody's something or did you really hear this information from somebody who could have had such information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who could have had such information, who was authorised for that. We just heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did the NATO bombing really happen? Was that correct information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: The planes were flying over and from there you could see that part where the Serbian army was going towards Srebrenica. I'm familiar with that area. We were going to a refugee camp there, but I think that I remember - I cannot be sure - that we saw smoke from these explosions and so on. I don't know whether these were bombs from aeroplanes or something else. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, are you able to tell us where you were at that point in time? Were you on the hill or the mountain with the letter V or were you in some other place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: You mean that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you saw this aviation, this bombing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Vijogor is a large area. It's like an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the population that was at Vijogor, was it receiving information from the army about what was happening at the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Maybe some were getting this information. I was just saying in my statement all the things that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you have been able to hear that without any of the senior officers saying that? Did it really happen that you were bombed by the planes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this hearsay or is it really true that NATO aeroplanes bombed positions of Republika Srpska? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, there were some portions that we could not see. We did not stay in the same spot all the time. For a while, we were in one part of Vijogor and we had one view, and then three or four hours later we were elsewhere and we could see smoke coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you could see smoke, plumes of smoke. Can you recall what day that was in relation to the day when you left your home, when you said goodbye to your sisters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure. It could have been the morning of the 11th; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, let me point you to line 35 of your statement. There, you say the following: "In the evening, the army command ordered all able-bodied men to go to Susnjari." Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: What do you mean did I see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, did you see that portion? Could you find it on the monitor? You can see there it says previously: "I saw the NATO aeroplanes flying over, dropping bombs but they -- they were expected to bomb the Serbian forces," and then it says, "The army command --" the next line: "In the evening, the army command ordered all able-bodied men ..." Can you see, the cursor is showing you where to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it reads there: "In the evening, the army command ordered all able-bodied men to go to Susnjari from Suceska too where there was a large number of men while all the women and children were supposed to go towards Potocari." So have you seen and read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question: How did you learn that there was an order issued that all able-bodied men should go to Susnjari whereas women --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, we probably heard it from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down a bit. You're using the same language as the witness and both speakers should pause between question and answer. It's otherwise very difficult for the interpreters. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the transcript that you can see before you, and once there is no more typing, once the typist stops, then you can answer my question. Now I will repeat my question: Did the army command really issue that order in the evening, relating to the separation of women and children and men, and ordering one group to go to Susnjari and the other to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, it is probable, it's probably so, they may have, but that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was that actually put in place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, a large number of men was leaving that camp, and leaving other villages in the Vijogor area, so men spent some time going up a mountain, which is before Susnjari, and then some separated, went to Potocari and Susnjari, because at the time it was impossible to go to Srebrenica directly, by a direct route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Whether that was implemented, that order, I really can't say, but they were headed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you please wait for my question. Did the families really get separated? Did the women -- or, rather, did the men go one way, in the direction of Susnjari, and the women the other way, to Potocari? Did that really happen, that separation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about my case, or my family's case, and some other families. These relatives of mine, they took the same decision, but nobody came and ordered them and said, "You line up there and you are going to go that way." It was just that we all went together, and then before Susnjari, in that village, people just decided, some, to go to Potocari, mainly the women and the children. Some went to Susnjari. But I never saw a soldier directing people where to go. I never saw anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you please listen to a portion of your statement, in lines 35, 36, and 37. I quote your words. You said: "In the evening, the army command ordered all able-bodied men to go to Susnjari from Suceska to where there was a large number of men, while all the women and children were supposed to go to Potocari." Now, my question is this: When you provided this statement, and this was right after the event, was your recollection of the events better than it is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I think I've already answered this question, but I will answer it again. We probably heard - that's what I said then, and I'm saying it again - we heard from someone, from some people or some women, I don't know, that the men would go to Susnjari and the women and children to Potocari. That's how it was. Whether this order came from the army command or not, I don't know, but we heard that it had. That's my answer. We heard it somehow, but how, exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard your answer. Now, my next question is: Right after this line, where it says that women and children were supposed to go towards Potocari, there is another sentence, and I will read it out to you and then I will put a question to you. "That night, below Susnjari, all members of the army and able-bodied men born after 1980 were lined up. I had not been a member of the army before. That evening, when the lineup took place, I was in the same company as my father Alija, who did not survive this exodus. That is, I've heard no news of him whatsoever." So my question, based on what you said there, is: You mention here the lineup below Susnjari of all able-bodied men. And this was done by the army. Can you recall that? And just a moment, I just want to finish my question. Now, do you remember that this -- these are your words, this is what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, I do. When I got there, my father was away. He had gone to fetch something from a house of some relatives. So when I got there, and my father, who was a member of that unit, although that's really a big question what to call it because he had neither a uniform nor any weapons, he never went to the front line, he spent all the time with us at home. Now, he was a member of some unit, I can't recall the number. There was a lineup there, I got there, and I just stayed around him. I stayed with him. And because these men were the army, they were armed, I thought that by going with him, I would save my skin. But when the shelling began, people started moving around, milling around, running, they wanted to get into the woods as soon as possible, and there I lost my father, I couldn't find him anymore, and although I tried to follow a soldier or be around a soldier nearby, actually I fell back and I stayed behind like everybody else while father went forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember, in the beginning, when Mr. McCloskey was putting questions to you, on page 6 of today's transcript, in line 2, he said that you were -- that the BH Army had ordered a column to be formed and that you went to the back part of the column whereas your father was in the front part of the column. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said before, I tried to stay with my father, but when the situation became chaotic it was just impossible to do that. All the civilians were trying to follow the troops. The soldiers didn't want to allow them because they were afraid they would step on a mine and get killed, and so the civilians fell back, and basically, that's my explanation. My father just went forward and I stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In today's transcript, in line 12, Mr. McCloskey talks about a column of armed BH soldiers and that there were also some armed soldiers at the end of the column. They were -- armed soldiers were at the head of the column and some were in the back of the column. So is that what the column looked like? Is that how it was lined up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, it was dark so you couldn't really see well. I tried to be as close to my father as I could. The column was moving forward, we were walking, and people were just saying the column is ahead of us. There were some 15.000 men there, it's a large number of men, and we walked like that some two or three kilometres, all the way to the morning. And when we reached the woods and when the shelling started, everyone started moving quickly forward. The civilians tried to push forward, but they stopped them. A unit remained behind and they said, "You stay behind. You will be at the end of the column." And that's how it happened. We remained in the back and that's how we continued walking. But until the shelling began, we kept moving in a line, but once the shelling started, all these soldiers moved past us. We were just standing there, we couldn't move or anything, we were afraid. They just passed us by and moved forward and we stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come to that, but would you please just answer my questions and then we will come to the points that you're trying to make which aren't really part of my question. So was your father in the forward part of the column and were you in the back of the column? And were there armed soldiers in front of the column and in the back of it? Just answer that question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I've already said it: When chaos broke out, people just lost their way and he just moved forward and I stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I tried to be short with this questioning of mine, and I was just trying to put some questions to you, but I will be forced to read out the words that -- from your statement that you've said before. I was just asking you whether your father was in the front and you stayed behind, because that's what it says in your statement. And your father was in the front because he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned weapons. Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, he was a soldier, he --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Where did I say that he had a weapon? Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'll read it to you in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: But where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, it's in your statement that you have on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can do that, but it's very difficult to go from line to line, so please answer my questions. As you can see, this is very closely typed, and it's hard to go from line to line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you this: My father was a soldier, but when he came back to Srebrenica, he never -- after the mobilisation, he -- after the demilitarisation, he stayed with us all the time. He never went to the front line, he never took part in combat. I never said -- I don't recall saying that he had a weapon, so don't impute things that I didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, but did your father have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I think I've answered that question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you just said that he didn't have a weapon and that he wasn't a soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, he was a soldier, but he didn't have a weapon. Had he been -- had he been armed, he might have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please sit closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now let us go to the part of the statement that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask you to move a little bit closer to the microphone. The Court Usher will assist you with the chair. There is something wrong with it, I think. It should be fixed. Now it's fixed, and when it happens again, please let us know. Mr. Tolimir, may I remind both speakers not to overlap again. It's very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could request that General Tolimir try not ask four-part questions. That's what got us into that last exchange, and if he does have some place in the document where he -- the witness has said his father had a gun, I think he should show it to the witness, because that also is obviously a sensitive point and if he's going to have things like that, I think he should show it to the witness or tell him he made a mistake, but that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would agree with the Prosecution to the last point. The witness has pointed out very clearly that his father was a soldier but he didn't have a weapon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if that is the case, why is it, then, that your father was separated from you and why did he go to the forward part of the column whereas you stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: He was -- he wasn't separated. He didn't get separated. But when the shelling started of this large crowd of people, some 15.000 men, we just lost track of each other. He went one way, I went the other, and we just couldn't find each other anymore. I cried out his name, I tried to find him, I called out his name. I was crying. I just tried to keep track, I tried to find him. No one separated us, it was just that in the chaos of the shelling, we just lost our way. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Because this statement is so closely typed and there are no paragraphs and there are many lines on a page, I can't really find the portion that I would like to point you to, but I will try to do it. So if you please bear with me, I will point out the part where I meant that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, you can find that spot, but it should not be in my statement. If need be, we can read the whole statement. I don't know how long it is. It's not too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right. So we can do it that way, but now, for now, please just answer my questions. Please look at line 48 on this same page that we have before us. Can you see it, where it says: "The column -- before we got to Kamenica we ran into a Chetnik ambush and the column got cut off there. I was toward the end of the column, almost at the very end because, in my estimate, there were some 1.000 people behind me. Everybody else was in front. The Chetniks were shelling, they were shooting from all sides, and so on."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, because I couldn't see where that is, could you please read it one more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show it to you. From the bottom, it's line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please look at the cursor, it's from the bottom, line 11 where you see the cursor there, the relevant portion is in the statement to be found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the entrance to Kamenica we ran into a Chetnik ambush, and there --" My apologies: "At the entrance to Kamenica we ran into a Chetnik ambush and the column was cut. I was near the end of the column because behind me there were about 1.000 men, I would say, while all the others were in front." So what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, you've just read that portion. Now, do you recall that? Would you please wait for my answer. You read out the sentence, whereas I didn't ask you to do that. So, now that you've read it, what can you tell us about the ambush that you ran into? What was happening from the moment you hit the ambush up until the moment you were out of it? What was -- what transpired there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: As the last part of the column was entering the woods, it was still relatively peaceful. There was no shelling at that point. However, when we started going downhill, along that wood, there was a column ahead of me and behind me. Suddenly, firing started and there was a stream -- I later realised that there was a stream at the foot of that hill. There was shooting, shooting broke out, people started crying out, things they were saying, that the Serbs had probably cut the column, and those who had weapons at that point moved forward. There was a lot of shooting. I don't know how long it was, but I believe we stayed -- the back -- we stayed there for about an hour or so, and then the shelling started. All kinds of fire could be heard. Smaller branches fell off trees because they were cut off by all the shooting. And then, after a while, the column moved forward again. When I reached the stream, I saw a lot of wounded and three or four dead people, and then the shelling continued, and it went on until nightfall. And then at times it would stop and then resume, and it went on all night until the morning, I believe. I don't know what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't want to interrupt you, but in answering my question you did not mention the number of dead, whereas in your statement in line 6, you say -- and that's line 6 on page 2 of your statement. Could we please have the next page, and then you will see in line 6. Here, we see it now. In line 6 from the top, it says, "300 to 500 were killed." This is line 7 in the English, also, where it says 300 to 500.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: So since the attack was ongoing, the whole time, when the ambush began, there was shelling and shooting the whole time, the wounded were falling constantly, moaning, there were dead people. After the shelling stopped in the morning, after that night, I could see five or six people dead around me. Some of them I knew by name. We were below one hill. When we crossed that hill during the day, after we began to surrender, then going past the dead I could see how many there were, because we were passing by dead people. There was some 300 [Realtime transcript read in error "500"] to 500, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did want to hear your estimate because you were an eyewitness. Can you now look at this other page that we are looking at, page 2, if you can look at line 18. The cursor will indicate where that is, and I'm going to read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Tolimir, on page 33, line 8, the last sentence of the answer of the witness reads, "There was some 500 to 500 in my estimate." I heard "some 300 to 500, in my estimate." Just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is an error. From 300 to 500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue -- before you continue, Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- and thank you, Judge Fluegge. This is not really a question because I'm comparing the statement of the witness. Witness, in your statement, you talked about a 300 to 500 civilians. You say that 300 to 500 civilians were killed, whereas in the transcript it is not clear. You only say that there were 300 to 500 people who were killed. So I would like to know if those were civilians or those were soldiers or is it altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anyone with arms -- weapons or in uniform among the dead. These two or three people that I knew, that were dead, were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were mostly civilians in that part of the column and that part of the column was mostly exposed to the shelling. Maybe there were some soldiers, but I'm just talking about things that I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And these civilians, as you say, were they able to serve and were they of an age that could be considered the age for people who were able-bodied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, they could have been considered able-bodied and well enough to serve. I don't know if they actually did. I'm just saying what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you know these people? Did you know if they were members of the army or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I think that that question doesn't make much sense. "Did you know 300 to 500 people?" Well, I knew some of those people. As for if I knew all of those people, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at line 18. "As I was running, I could see buses where there were women." Perhaps this could be indicated by the cursor. "As we were running, we could see buses where there were women."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "They were crying, they were being transported and the buses were moving towards Konjevic Polje." On the basis of what I read to you just now, my question is: Were you running along the same road and going in the same direction that the buses were travelling on with the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: We were going on the same -- we were on the same road but we were going in different directions. The buses were going towards Kladanj, Zvornik and Konjevic Polje. They were going towards Konjevic Polje. They couldn't pass by us, and then we were ordered to run towards Bratunac, so we and the buses passed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please tell us whether you and the others who were there, was it illogical for you for your mothers, sisters, and so on to be riding in buses while you were being mistreated in such a way running next to those buses while they were inside, crying? Did you ask yourself why that happened that the army would treat brothers and sisters differently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: What do you mean "differently"? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will clarify. You were seeing buses in which there were mothers and women crying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Can you please wait for me to finish so that we don't overlap. They were crying because they saw you as you were running, and because you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now tell the Trial Chamber, how is it that the same army, the Serbian army, that captured you was transporting these women and children and was taking you to a different side in a different direction as prisoners? Thank you. Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I don't see any difference, because we were later loaded up on the same trucks that they were on. I don't see any difference. Later, when we were coming back from Bratunac, I could see buses going behind us, so the same people were there who were being transported from Potocari, they were behind us, and they ended up in front of the same school. What is the difference? Perhaps these trucks were more comfortable as they were being driven on them. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have an objection to such questions as asking for the motivations of the VRS in this kind of context. How would this witness begin to know the motivations of the VRS? This is an invitation to an argument, which, at this stage, I don't think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have received an answer from the witness, from his point of view, and from his observations he could make. Mr. Tolimir, go ahead, please, for some minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Whether it's logical or illogical, I did ask you and you did answer. The Trial Chamber appreciates the answer, the objection. My following question is: Were these buses stopped? Did you see them stopping in that section of the road that you were going along in the opposite direction? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: They couldn't pass next to us, so then when we started running, these trucks and buses were going behind us. But I can tell you my aunt saw me and later she told my mother: "I saw him. I saw him standing on the asphalt with his hands in the air. He will probably survive. He will be in a camp somewhere or something like that. But many who were in Potocari were taken away and they are gone. They are not here anymore. He perhaps will survive." So my mother waited. She thought I was captured somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, please answer my question and we will come to that later. Can you please tell me, did you see in that sector where you were running, were buses stopped and why? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Because they couldn't pass by us. If you're thinking specifically in that place where we were, Sandici, where we were out on the asphalt, is that what you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of those people who were with you got into a -- get into a bus? Were they put onto a bus, anybody who was below 18 in the Sandici area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: When we got to the meadow in Sandici, a Serbian soldier who was giving a speech and explaining where we would be going, that we would be exchanged, that we would be going to Bratunac to a hangar, that we will not have dinner and then, when our authorities looked for us, we would be exchanged. There were many of my peers there, people of my age, younger men, there were wounded among us. They asked is there anybody there who is younger, who was born after 1980 or later? These were boys, and they went. I didn't see if they got into buses or trucks, but they left the crowd. Also, a boy replied he was 11, and they said, "No." I also wanted to say something, but this boy who was told, "No, you can't come with us," then I changed my mind. I could see that some of my peers weren't allowed to leave, so I decided not to draw attention to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what the Prosecutor spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have to break now. We will have our first break and we will resume quarter past 4.00. The Court Usher will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on. Bear in mind, please, not to overlap, and we would appreciate if you could put short questions to the witness. It would help the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we talked about how, on the road near Sandici, the Serbian army allowed those people who were born before 1980 -- after 1980, to get on the buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I told you what the soldier said, how many boys entered, and that this was not something that was permitted to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You said what you've said. The Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, on page 7, line 13, said that those who were born after 1980 were permitted to leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the soldier said. That's what the soldier said. Three boys left. One of them later, who was much younger than the others, also put his hand up, but he couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name of this younger boy? Do you know anything about him? Since you spent one day with him, do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can we now look at this page now, please. Page 2 of your statement. Can we look at line 12, from the top. Six lines from below -- down from where it says, "300 to 500," where it says 100 metres. Do you see 100 metres in that line? "They lined us up on that asphalt road in five rows." I'm quoting: "They lined us up on that asphalt road about five rows, each about 100 metres in length. Anybody who had anything put it down beside the tank, and so on and so forth." Do you see this part that I'm reading out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, if you were lined up in five rows, was it possible that those five lines that were 100 metres long numbered 5.000 people? They didn't count you, they didn't place you in rows, one next to each other. Is this possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the asphalt where we were lined up. It's about 100 to 150 metres long, that part, so there were some five rows on one lane. The wounded were lying in front of us, in front of those rows. I'm taking into account the wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: In your estimate, how many people were there in Sandici? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: First in Kamenica and then later we ran to Sandici, it was approximately 1.000 to 2.000 people. This is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we now look at the statement in e-court, 65 ter 06671.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is all sealed so it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to broadcast it, thank you. Thank you. This first statement that we looked at, I would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we are looking at your second statement, that you gave after the events in August 1995. The statement shouldn't be broadcast. Let's look at page 2 of this statement, thank you, so that you can follow what I'm saying. First of all, we are going to look at paragraph 5. Can you please read it? This is something that I was supposed to tell you, about the forming of the column: "A very long column was formed, and around 11 July in the evening, we started moving. 11 July in the evening. I was toward the end of the column with all the civilians. B and H soldiers guided us at the front of the column. Since my father was in the army, he was toward the front. This was the last time I saw my father. Today I do not know where he is." My question is, since I said that he was with a rifle, I made a mistake, was your father placed at the front because he was a soldier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: When I lost him, probably he went to the front. That's probably when he went to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement of yours accurate, since you say "probably" or can it be questioned as to its accuracy since now you are denying that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: What am I denying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat: When the column was formed, you said, "Since my father was in the army, he was at the front." You were not talking about getting lost, losing each other here. And you say, "That is the last time that I saw my father," but at the top you said: "I was towards the end of the column with the other civilians. B and H soldiers guided us at the front of the column." My question was: Was your father at the front of the column because you had lost each other or because he was a soldier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: When I lost him, since the soldiers were going to the front, 99 per cent was that he went to the front, and the rest of us civilians ended up where we ended up. He was found in Nova Kasaba, however. So definitely he had gone to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Why did you get separated from you -- from your father? Are you able to answer that question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this question was put to the witness several times already and he explained it in detail. There is no need to repeat that again. Please move to another topic and put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please, are you able to explain the difference between what you have just said and what is stated in this statement? Are the facts entered into the statement erroneously? Who wrote this statement that we are reading on the screen right now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should be more precise. You just say a difference. The difference between what you have just said and the -- and what is stated in the statement. If you see a difference, you should be very precise and put that to the question -- put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to put a shorten and clear question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a difference between what you have just said now about you getting separated from your father and what is stated in paragraph 5 of the statement that you gave in August 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I don't see any essential difference there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 6 -- or my apologies, paragraph 5, in line 1, you say that around 16 or 1700 hours on the 12th of July, Chetniks started shooting and shelling at some point in the forest. My question is: Was it the Chetniks who were at some point in the forest or was it you that were there at the time indicated on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, the question is a bit long. Could you please just repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is, in fact, paragraph 6 and not paragraph 5. Please repeat your question in a short way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, the first two lines of paragraph 6, in them it is unclear who was in the forest when the shooting started around 16 or 1700 hours, and if you can tell us where the shooting was coming from and where you were as opposed to those who were shooting, thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, when the shooting started, the column stopped for about an hour or so. There was shooting and there were shells landing. They were probably fired from the hill, and we could hear Serbs shouting, "Where are you heading, Balijas? Come back, where are you going?" There were -- the bullets were whizzing past us. We could hear them, and we could also hear the sound of the shells landing, but where it was fired from we couldn't really see it from the forest because we were inside the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted to hear from you. So in other words, you couldn't really see the place from which the fire was coming.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, we were in the woods but we heard the Serbs calling each others out, and bullets were flying around, branches were falling off trees, they were cut down by bullets, and I assume that the shooting was coming from uphill because of the lie of the land there. We were near a stream and there were hills around and I assumed they were shooting from up there, from the higher ground. And those who were calling out, I think they were also calling out from the hills, the surrounding hills, so it wasn't close by, it was a bit farther off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The situation that you described a moment ago, that was around 16 or 1700 hours on the 12th of July. When was it that you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: We surrendered on the 13th of July. So after the 12th of July, we spent the night in the forest, during that shelling, and then in the morning, when we heard Serb soldiers calling out, using loudspeakers, that was the 13th, so we came out on the 13th. It was probably sometime in the afternoon. We were -- we spent some five to six hours -- or we came to the meadow around 5.00 or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 5, paragraph 2, line 1, you say the following in lines 1 and 2: "He said that they were from Serbia and that they would transport us to hangars in Bratunac until ours [as interpreted] (and I assumed that he meant the BH government) asks for you -- ask for you." Now, my question is this: Is this individual who said these words, did you see that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. He had overalls and a black bandana around his head, tied in the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- can you describe the uniform? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform, one-piece uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did those soldiers have any insignia on their uniforms showing that they were members of the army or anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your question, but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to say, and I quote: "I could not hear him that clearly. I have never heard anyone from Serbia talk, and I'm not familiar with any particular dialect. I clearly heard him say, 'We are from Serbia.' He said they would continue to search for people and, if found, those people would be killed. I stopped listening to him," and so on and so forth. You go on, I end the quote there. So my question is this: In view of this paragraph and based on his words, him saying that he was from Serbia, you concluded that they were all from Serbia; is that correct? So were they all from Serbia because he said that he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, what I said in my statement was what I had heard. Now, whether they were from Serbia or not, I don't know. I was just saying there what he said, what he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you go on to say that you had never seen those people who had held you there in custody in the area, but that you were familiar with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: I did not recognise a single soldier anywhere, which doesn't mean that they weren't there. Maybe there were some, but I did not recognise anyone. Not only there, but also later on, I never recognised any face, but there were people who recognised some of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, would you please take a look at paragraph 5, the first two sentences: "As I sat in the meadow, I saw a house burning nearby with some Chetniks on the balcony. The soldier wearing the black bandana ordered us to lie face down on our stomachs. Shooting started about 100 to 200 metres from where I lay." Please tell us, did the shooting started while you were in Sandici or are you talking about something else there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: When we were ordered -- while we were in the meadow, when we were ordered to lie down on our stomachs and not to raise our heads and look around, that we should put our arms behind our heads and clap our hands and that we should say -- call out, "Long live the king, long live Serbia," and we spent some five hours there. There was shooting all around us, I could not see who was shooting, what they were shooting at, but you could hear the echo of the shooting in that valley there. When we were ordered to stand up, I saw soldiers shooting into a house which was not far from where we were, and that was a Muslim house. It had been burned down and he was shooting into the house. I don't know whether there was anyone there, who was there, but an uncle of mine told me that a neighbour of ours who lived nearby, that he was sitting in the house and that he couldn't see him sitting anymore, so most probably they took the wounded there to kill them, to finish them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that your assumption, your conclusion, or your knowledge, based on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, what is certain is that there were no wounded there, so I assumed that they were killed off there.
