utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, please look at paragraph 3 on page 5 that we have before us. I quote: "I'm familiar with this area because it was nearby. I did not recognise any of the soldiers come -- as coming from this area, and if they were the Bosnian Serb army, I believe I would have recognised some of them." Now, my question is this: How would you recognise soldiers if they were -- if they were members of the Serb army, Bosnian Serb army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, that unit, maybe they were Serbs, maybe not, maybe they were Bosnian Serbs, maybe not, but I didn't recognise a single face. Now, if one of them had been a neighbour from around where we were, I would have recognised him, but I did not recognise anyone. However, later on, outside the school, there were people who recognised some of those soldiers. As we were getting off the bus outside the school, and as they were beating people one after another, one of those soldiers, Serb soldiers, asked a man whether -- "Do you recognise me?" And the man answered, "Yes, I do, brother." And then this soldier started beating him and asked him, "What do you mean you know me?" implying that he shouldn't really acknowledge that he knew him. And they beat him badly. They beat him up. They beat him with rifle butts, with their feet, kicked him, they beat him up really badly. I did not get any beating but they beat everyone who passed through there. And then later on, when we were in the classroom, one of them was saying that there was a neighbour of his there, or maybe a co-worker, I don't recall whether he was from Zvornik or so, but I believe -- but the man who was beaten up, he was from Zvornik and that was his neighbour, a soldier from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on this, the fact that this person recognised this other soldier, was it based on that that you concluded that these were soldiers of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already answered this question. I myself did not recognise any of the soldiers, but that should not mean that they were or weren't members of the VRS. I just know of the story where this other man recognised one of the soldiers, and that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that people who had been expelled from other parts of Bosnia had come there, for instance from Kladanj, Tuzla, Olovo, those people were expelled to the territory of Republika Srpska and then they became soldiers of the VRS? Could it be that that was the reason why you didn't recognise them, because they had come from those areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-008
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I cannot do guesswork here, I can only tell you what I saw. Now, whether these people came from Kladanj or Sarajevo or Serbia, I don't know. I just told you about what I had occasion to see. I did not see anyone I knew, which doesn't mean that there weren't any people from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I asked you is that we have your statement, and if we leave it as it is, it can lead us to a faulty conclusion, and we are here in trial, and I just wanted to clear some things up with you and ask you to clear them up. And my apologies if I was too insistent, and I will not put any more questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would object to statements that are not questions, especially ones that are just critical of the witness for I don't know why. That just is argumentative and is not appropriate. There's been several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness, and my apologies personally to you because maybe somebody else could have cleared that up as to where these people were from, but let's not go there now. Now, I want -- I won't ask -- I won't put any questions about what Mr. McCloskey had asked you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, again and again you are putting statements on the record. I have to remind you that it is up to the Chamber to give weight to all evidence before the Chamber, to the testimony of witnesses, to documents, and so on. It's not, at this point in time, not your duty to do that. Please put questions to the witness and wait for the answer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies to you and to the Prosecutor for being irritated by my manner of questioning because I'm not a lawyer, but I just wanted -- also my apologies to the witness but I just wanted to tell the witness that I was not going to put any questions about those parts where the witness was emotional. And I thank you, Witness, and my apologies for having to put questions to you to clarify the situation. Thank you and may God bless you and have a safe trip home. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness and I thank everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were very clear and, in fact, I don't really have any questions for you but I would just like to check one thing. On the transcript, at page 6, line 24, of the transcript of today, you talked about people who were with you in the column and who killed themselves, who would have committed suicide. Can you please tell me, how did these people commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a clarification on the record? That was part of the summary of the previous statements and testimony of the witness given by the Prosecutor. But nevertheless, the question is clear: How did these people commit suicide? Can you give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in the forest was unbearable. It was very difficult. And I saw a man who actually -- who put a hand grenade and set it off and blew himself up. Now, why he did that, when one thinks in retrospect of what was to happen later on, then perhaps it's something we can understand. He probably did not want to surrender, because some other people who had their wits about them, maybe more, or were more cool-headed, they had fled and they actually survived. I know some people like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I understand, of course, that those were very difficult times. But I would like to know the following: Would it have been possible for the people who were in the column to bury those who had committed suicide, or was it not possible at all at the time of the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were so many wounded people that nobody really paid attention to the -- those who were dead. People who knew other people who were wounded -- for instance, I helped carry a man who had -- whose leg was broken, and all the time while I was there with my uncle, I wasn't really afraid of getting killed. I was afraid of getting wounded and being left behind, because -- and suffering there, because in that situation, when there was all that shooting, so no one was thinking. People just tried, those who were wounded, they just tried to find someone who could help carry them because if there was no one you knew when you were wounded, you would just be left behind, and that was my greatest fear, getting wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber would like to thank you that you came to The Hague again. It was a very tough day for you. You went through all the emotions again of the events you have been in. Thank you very much that you came to The Hague, that you assisted us to find out the truth, and now you are free to return to your normal activities. The court officer will assist you leaving the courtroom, but first we have to go into closed session to enable you to leave the courtroom without lifting your identity. Thank you very much again, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn back into open session first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender 65 ter 06671, that's the second statement that we saw, into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00140, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I take it that you are going to call Witness Gallagher now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it is. As you know from the motion that you ruled on last week, she should be here, coming through the door momentarily. She may be in the witness room, waiting, and we -- it's hard to tell how long this is going to take because I'm going to go through some of this book, but we, as you know, we have Colonel Boering set for tomorrow because of the Dutch interpreters but, yes, she should be here, ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You please can give me information. Are we still in examination-in-chief with this witness in this portion of her testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a new area that -- and I thank the general and Mr. Gajic for agreeing to allow us to discuss the -- and have her testify beginning in direct. This is a -- as you'll recall from the motion, there is an exhibit that is already in evidence, and it's what we refer to as "the duty officer notebook." It's 361. It's the duty officer notebook from the Zvornik Brigade that you have seen references from this book from the key dates in question. Witnesses were questioned about it and you had questions about it, and so we have accelerated our presentation so that you can -- well, we can fill the gap and that you can see an exhibit that we had created, much like Mr. Blaszczyk's road book, which is a portion of the duty officer logbook where the investigation has identified the various dates the investigation believes that pages in the logbook refer to, which is of course crucial, and some of the entries, the investigation has identified who wrote those entries, as well as some other information in that. And we think that this exhibit is -- would be very helpful as more witnesses talk about these events, and you will hopefully have that -- this booklet to refer to, especially during some rather key witnesses. And so she is beginning to talk about that. She's basically here just to give us a -- the briefest of background on this document, since there will be other VRS officers that really know much more about the document, but -- and then to just tell us what the investigation determined about what dates pages are on and what people were there. I don't wish, nor will I ask her to analyse or evaluate or provide any opinion about the substance of the material in that. That is not her mandate in this situation but just to help guide us on what -- how the investigation determined the dates and ID'd the people in it, which are key to understanding this document as more witnesses testify about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this update, and now I'm back. And that happens sometimes with the OTP witnesses, the investigators of the OTP, that we are not very clear in which part of the testimony we are. Now we are commencing a new examination-in-chief, if I understood you correctly, in relation to the new witness summary we have received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe the -- it was agreed that we -- this would be direct -- direct testimony only and so that the general would have time prepare for any cross-examination at a later date because, as I said, they were -- we were very happy that they were agreed to us that, within this relatively short time frame, to help fill this gap with this important document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to assist in the record, Mr. President, the -- what we refer to as the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook is -- the full copy of that, or the actual original, and we have the original here for you to look at, is P14. We have given this portion of this -- of the logbook the number 65 ter 361A. And, Mr. President, we have -- the general and Mr. Gajic have hard copies. If we could provide you hard copies as well, I think it will be -- it will be helpful because this works -- it works with the computer but it's a bit more helpful to have actually a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Surprisingly, I just received one from the Bench before me but it would be helpful to give these, with the Court Usher's assistance, to all participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we provided one to your attorney, so we have two for -- two more now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Gallagher, welcome back to the courtroom. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony in September still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has more questions for you. Mr. McCloskey, please commence your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good evening, Ms. Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- I think you probably caught the last end of what I had just explained, but can you first just tell us, briefly, what P14 is, what we call the duty officer notebook of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original duty officer notebook, which is what I'm holding before me, is a notebook that was used by the Zvornik Brigade and written in by the duty officer or the assistant duty officer, and this particular notebook was written in between the dates of May 29th, 1995, and July 27th, 1995. And as you'll see, it will be notes, contemporaneous notes, reminders, messages, anything that's coming in through the brigade that needs to be communicated to the commander, to the Chief of Staff, to other battalions, reports that the duty officer has to write himself. So it's basically -- it's a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us just the briefest description of what you've learned a duty officer for the brigade is. What is just his basic job?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer is always a member of the brigade command, so it's an officer who is posted 24 hours at the brigade headquarters and they are -- they keep an eye on what's happening in the field, what's happening with the battalions, with other brigades, with the units. They pass information on to -- back and forth up and down to the -- to the commanders, to the Chief of Staff, and lower to the battalions themselves, and basically keeping everybody informed of what's happening, and they also can transmit and relay orders and reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Gallagher, as it happens sometimes with B/C/S-speaking witnesses, please slow down while speaking. We understand you but, on the other hand, there is interpretation in different languages, and please pause between question and answer. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Gallagher, you mentioned the dates of the duty officer notebook that you have before you. Before I get into that, can you tell us where the investigation received this original book that you have before you, this -- which -- if you could hold that up so they can just get an idea of this green book. Can you explain where -- how we got -- how the investigation received this?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received it from Dragan Obrenovic himself, who was Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and he had -- his attorney had provided it to the OTP at the time of his plea agreement in June 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the actual demonstrative exhibit which has the number of 65 ter 361A, what dates does this demonstrative exhibit cover, from the actual duty officer notebook? Is it the whole notebook, a portion thereof; can you just give us that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's only a portion of the original notebook. It is only the dates from July 11th to through July 24th, and as I mentioned, the original notebook is from May 29th to July 27th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's start with that 361A, this product. How is this sort of colloquially referred to on the investigative team?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it's "the duty officer notebook." It has had a number of different names over the years but, as you see from the title, duty officer notebook. Sometimes you hear "duty officer logbook."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this is just a title provided by the office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So this particular first page, that's the title that was given to it by the Office of the Prosecutor, so let's go to the second page, which should be page 3 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can add something, it also gets referred to as "the teacher's edition of the notebook."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do we call this -- this exhibit the teacher's edition?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you will see, it's not exclusively just the original notebook that has been colour copied onto here. There is an English translation and some explanations of the notebook itself; who has written in it, what dates, and sometimes some explanations of abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just -- before we get to the foreword, let's just give an example of what it looks like. Perhaps let's go to -- should be page 9 in the e-court, and I don't know if e-court will show the B/C/S and the English. If we can try to do that so we can see how the book lays out. It would be page 8 in the -- in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was told that we have only the English version in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we all have the B/C/S in front of us, and the book, it's a combination of English and B/C/S, so you don't go to another one. It's page 8 in this exhibit. I don't know if you can put page 8 and page 9 in e-court next to each other. Yes, that's page 8, and, I don't know, can you put page 9 next to it? That you're basically recreating the book as we have it in front of us. And the purpose of these questions, it's not so important to be able to read it, just to show how the book works for someone that's using it. That's a good start. If you go to page 8 and 9, you'll get exactly what we want. Right. And we see that the ERNs are both matching, so those pages match.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So can you tell us what is on the left and what is on the right in -- which is up on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the left side is a colour copy of the original duty officer notebook. Nothing has been touched on it, it is as you see it in its original that I have with me. On the right side you see the English translation of that same page, and you'll notice that there are some of the numbers and some notations are in colour. That means that that's what has been added by the -- our team, by the OTP, and is not on the original version. Such as the date, and you'll see the notations in both red and green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go back to page 3, the foreword, which describes how this works, and we'll go over that carefully so it -- so you can get some explanations on it now. But if everyone could keep the book open and perhaps on the pages we just were, it will help make more sense. Okay. So in the foreword, we can read it, that: "The exhibit provides an English translation of the duty officer notebook of the Zvornik Brigade from 11 July 1995 through 23 July 1995. The exhibit presents the B/C/S colour copy of the original on the left-hand side and the corresponding translation of that page in English on the right-hand side." So I take it this is what we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "Prosecution made every attempt to replicate the layout and appearance of the original notebook in the English translation." What did we mean by that and how will we see that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll see that the lines and the spacing replicate what is in the original. If anything has been underlined, if anything has been circled, that also has been done in the English version. Any particular marks, dashes, that sort of thing, punctuation, has also been replicated in the right side, so it's made to look exactly, as much as possible, as it is on the -- in the original so it's easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it goes on to say that: "In addition, the Prosecution has provided additional markings on the English translation, indicating the author of the notations, the date of the notations, and other information." So when we say the author of the notations in this book, what are we referring to or who are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be the notations that are made by the duty officers themselves or else by the assistant duty officers, so anyone who has written in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say duty officers and assistant duty officers. How, roughly, have you learned that worked in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was largely the duty officer that did the main work and, as I mentioned, who was a brigade command officer. The assistant duty officer was lower-ranking and usually they spelled the duty officer while he slept or rested or was away from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that's the author of the notations. And then the date of the notations, how was this book organised by chronology and date? If it was.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book is organised and written as like a date book, as chronologically, and the duty officers and assistant duty officers usually wrote the date in the notebook themselves. There are some places where we have, as you'll see, in red, we have put in a date when we thought the date has changed or, as you'll learn soon, when Dragan Obrenovic believed a date had changed and added that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's -- and then it says, "The date of the notations and other information below," then it says, in red text, ERN numbers. Okay, we all know what ERN numbers are at this point. The author, which you've explained, the date. And it says, "And markings by Dragan Obrenovic," with a star, and then we look down at the star, and the star says, "Dragan Obrenovic made certain markings in pencil in preparation for his trial in 2003." Can you explain that, these pencil markings of Dragan Obrenovic that are referenced here?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he turned the original notebook over to the OTP, he had it in his possession for a while from when the Drina Corps archives were -- Drina Corps collection was being moved and it had been moved in Mali Zvornik, and at that time he had obtained this notebook in 1999 and he had, in preparation for his trial here, he had gone through the notebook and made some -- some markings, some small markings in pencil. They were almost exclusively the date and then, in a couple of places, who he knew the duty officer to be at that time. So you'll see in here and we have notated in the book any time that he has written in pencil in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that pencil, does that stand out very well in this colour photocopy?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it's not easy to tell when -- in the original, in the colour copy that we have in the exhibit, that it's pencil or pen. We've notated it on the English side so that you're not mistaken at all. In the original duty officer notebook, itself, it's quite obvious that it's in pencil because everything else is written in pen, so that's very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when we get to one of those sections we can hand the book up. All right. Then it goes on to say that: "Dates noted in red on the left margin of the page indicate the place in the notebook where the date changed from one day to another. However, due to insufficient information, the precise date change could not always be ascertained and in this case we have noted the date in red italics." So you've said this is a chronological book, but how do you explain that there is not dates? What are you doing with these red italics?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, you will see dates written in on the original notebook. But they don't always write in when the date changes, from let's say, July 12th to the 13th. You'll see the times on the 12th might go up to 11.00, 11.30 at night, and then the next entries will be at 3.30 in the morning, 4.30 in the morning, and the duty officer or assistant has not notated that now we are talking July 13th, so what we've done is added that date change in ourselves on the English version in red italics on the left side of the margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that an approximation or is it, in your view, exact, when we put it in there?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an approximation. You'll see as we go through it, you won't be able to know exactly when it changed, so you'll see that it's now 3.30 in the morning the next day, and so at that point, when we know that it has changed to the next day, we've made a notation in the red italics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now you have mentioned that there are dates written down, or sorry, times -- excuse me, times written down in this book, and before we get and actually see some examples, can you give us just generally what -- why -- how is it that times are written down in this book?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oftentimes late in the evening or early in the morning, the battalions and different units will report in as to their situation out in the field. So you will see those early morning times often each day. Other times, there will be when somebody or a unit needs a wake-up call, so oftentimes you'll see a 0430 wake-up call for someone. If somebody is going to be coming to the brigade headquarters, they will make a note of it, if something is going to be delivered at a certain time, they will make a note of it. So a variety of reasons you'll see times written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were some of the times that you were -- just referred to able -- were you able to evaluate whether those times were actually of the present when they were writing it down as opposed to future time, something to be done in the future?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It's fairly evident in the notebook, when you see it, that -- where it will say, you know, a wake-up call at 0430 to somebody and that will have been written at 2 in the morning, versus something that is past tense that something was done at 8 p.m., so it's fairly obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know you'll get to this as well but can you tell us generally what sources of information from the investigation were -- did the investigation use to determine the author and the date in some situations? Just generally.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it's from the duty officers themselves that have identified when they were the duty officer, when they wrote in the notebook in their own handwriting, other witnesses' statements and testimony as well, and then in some cases it has been from a handwriting expert. In addition, just to assist in corroborating who had written in the notebook, we also cite, in the back of the book, combat reports, any reports and intercepts that confirm when someone wrote in the book or who the duty officer was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll go over a few pages to get examples of this, so let's go to the next page, which should be -- well, there is another page, page 5, in the exhibit, on e-court. I apologise, if we could go back to page 3, and I know it's not in B/C/S, so I will read out that last section so the general is fully apprised of this English page. The one part I left out was that noted in green text, where it says, "Green text" in green ink: "Illegibles and additional explanations from the translator have been written in green ink to highlight that they are not part of the original notebook." Can you explain that a bit?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Since it's a handwritten notebook, there will be in a few places a word that was illegible, either due to handwriting or perhaps faintness, so that has been notated in the English version. Also, there is a couple of places where an abbreviation or something has been explained, such as "PB," it will show in the English version "light infantry brigade," or "VMA" will be a medical academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, now we can go to page 5 in the e-court. And again, in English in red, at the top, we see Glossary of Terms. On the left side we will see the Serbian abbreviations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the English meaning of those abbreviations, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did this information regarding the abbreviations come from?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that CLSS has put together and has given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page, page 7 in e-court. This is an ERN ending 5619. And what's this?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the cover of the original duty officer notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if you look very closely at this, I'm not sure it shows up very well but is there some kind of writing on the front of that original?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It is difficult to see, and I think almost impossible on the screen, but it shows in pen it's written, "29 of May, 1995" and I think it should be "27 of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let's now go to -- well, where we were, at page -- page 8 and 9 up on the screen, if we could. And I think we should all open our books to that -- to that page. And the first thing we see in the -- if we could switch that to the left and right so it's identical to the book. I'm not sure, after 5.30, it's probably better to have it the same as it is in the actual book. Thank you. Okay. Perfect. So now in looking at the right side, page 9 in e-court, we see in red, 10/11 July 1995. What's the significance of that? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means on this page you'll have some notation that's from July 10th as well as July 11th. So it's the switchover of dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see down in the left-hand side of the same page, in italics, 11 July, and can you explain, just remind us what that means, that italics, 11 July?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means it's something that has been added by the OTP, it's not in the original, and it is our estimate of the date at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were -- how were you able to determine that that was the changeover time, or the approximate changeover time, as you've said?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'll see to the right side where it does say, 11 July 1995, so that was already written in in the original notebook. And then just above it, the line above it, you see the 0400 hours. If you go up another six lines or so, you'll see some times of 2300 hours and 2310 hours. And we know that earlier it's 10 July, so that's 2300 hours, 2310 hours on the 10th, and then at 0400 hours we are now into the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now looking at the number -- the Serbian version on the left side, we can all see 11.07.95. Can you look in the original book on that, just to double check for us. It's ERN 5728, and can you describe for us what you see there, in terms of ink and pencil?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do see it written in in blue ink; however, it's underlined in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we switch over and look at the English again, there has been an OTP indication, "Underlines in pencil by Dragan Obrenovic." So can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- as he told us in his statement, he had underlined some of the dates or written in some dates when -- as he was preparing for his trial, so he told us at that time that he had underlined in pencil this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could show that, perhaps, to the Defence, if they would like to see that. This is the only way to see it, and there will be more pencil marks, so I think it's a good thing to see, and if the Court would like to see it as well and perhaps hold onto it because there will be a couple more pencil marks that we would like to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you want to see that at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to know right now what it is that is written down above the date 11th July 1995, because it's a different handwriting. So who was it who added that and how are we to know that it wasn't added by somebody else subsequently and that the purpose of it wasn't that they should actually exonerate themselves thereby?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey may deliver that during his examination-in-chief, but the question was different: Do you want to see the original notebook now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Well, if I can't know the difference -- if I cannot have the explanation that I asked for, then I really can't add anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original notebook should be given to the Defence by the Court Usher, please, and then later to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could hold it open to where it is, I think Mr. Gajic should be able to see the pencil marks. And the general, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Based on -- well, in part on what the general said, let me ask you this: Did -- did the investigation determine all of the various entries in this and where -- who wrote them?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you'll see, there is a -- quite a number of places where we don't know who wrote in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the particular point that the general was interested in, the term above 11 July, and I think we can look over at the English and see that that says, "Strbac, 0400 hours." Did -- are you aware if the investigation has identified who wrote that and when?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We haven't identified who wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, let's just continue and go to the next page. If we could put up 10 and 11 the same way you've very nicely done that before. If we could get English on the right and Serbian on the left again would be nice. Or number 10 e-court on the left and number 11 on the right. Okay. Thank you. Now, we -- first thing we see as we look at the top of this English translation, 11 July 1995, and how was that determined?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- from the page before. It had been written in 11 July, and then if you follow the times, then you'll see 0600 hours or 10.00 a.m., so we are still on the same date of 11 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original notebook should be given back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next thing we see is date in pencil by Dragan Obrenovic, and actually, if we -- if we blow up that B/C/S or the Serbian side up in the right-hand corner, it may help us identify that, but can you just briefly explain that? Yeah, that's a nice blowup, so it looks --

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic himself told us that he had written in the date of 11 July 1995, when he was reviewing the notebook and just making a note of when a date was or a date changed in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as we look down this English page, we see an entry in green, and before that entry we see the abbreviations "KPVT" and then a little note, "heavy machine-gun." Can you remind us why there is green in here?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it's an explanation of an abbreviation or something that needs further explanation or if there is anything illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page in the hard copy, and that's number 12 and number 13 in e-court. And we have the English and they are both up there now. So we now see, as we are doing the same thing, we see 11/12 July. So what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It includes both the 11th and the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we go over, down the page to the left, we see this italics 12 July, and how is it that you determined that that was the approximate date change -- or excuse me, yeah, date changeover?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's an estimate of when it became July 12th. If you look further down at the bottom, you'll see the times of 0345, 0346, so we know for sure it's the 12th of July then. And the estimate as to why it may have changed to the 12th earlier than that is that generally the orders and the requests from the units happen very late in the evening or early in the morning of the next day. And if you go above that, then you see that it's 1900 hours and 1910 hours, from the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's turn the page again and now go to 14 on the left side and 15 on the right side in e-court. And we see 12 July, so in your view are we still on 12 July, based on that red?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see, over in the B/C/S, and of course in the English, 12 July 1995 written with a partial box underneath it. And does that help you indicate the date as well?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there any indication that Obrenovic had anything to do with that date?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. There is nothing written in pencil in the original on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So -- well, like the general said, unless someone has come in and added material or added things into this book since it was used, what would that date represent?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents that that is on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now for the first time, as we go down the English side, we see red brackets and the name Milan Maric, and it's around just a small portion, and what can you tell us about that? How was that determined?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that we believe it was Milan Maric who wrote that section. He told the OTP that he was the duty officer starting at 0800 hours on the morning of the 12th. Other people have also confirmed that he was the duty officer at that time, including Dragan Obrenovic and his -- the duty officer that relieved him later, Sreten Milosevic. And he also had written a -- there is another logbook, it's an operational diary that the duty officers write in each day, and it's more formal and it's more of what happened during the day, including the handing over to the next duty officer. So he signs his name, and that handwriting which he had told us -- just below that passage that he had told us that he had written in that day was used to compare to the handwriting in this section. And so the two were believed to be the same and that he wrote that particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn the page, 16 and 17 in e-court. And what date are we on here?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are still on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again we see everything on that page, according to the bracket, was written by Milan Maric, based on what the investigation has uncovered?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is Milan Maric alive?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did he die, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn the next page, 18 and 19 in e-court. And again we see 12 July and Milan Maric. Anything different in the analysis?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how can you base that? How do you know they haven't switched to another date, or why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll see that the times still are going chronologically, you know, by time. You have 1350 hours and then 1440 hours, so there has been no indication that the time has changed to past midnight, so we are still on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, number 20 and 21. Again we see same as the 12th, and Milan Maric, and again how do you know that this is the same date?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reason; the times are still going sequentially, getting later and later in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see some green written here, the illegibles that you referred to and some of the abbreviations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I see it's break time and just so you knew, my plan was to go through each page up until the 14th to give you a feel for some of those important days, and then skip to each day as they switched and why she feels that's the day that it switched, so it should be -- it should go much quicker after we get up to the 14th. It shouldn't take very long, now that I think we are all familiar with how this fairly basic document works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We should have our second break now and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can we now -- we are just, as a reminder, we are on 12 July, Milan Maric is writing everything, but now let's just -- let's skip on e-court to page 26 and page 27, but I think the hard copy we can just flip through the pages slowly and I think you'll see that it's still the 12th of July, Milan Maric, as we go through the pages leading up to e-court 26 and 27, where we now see 12 and 13 July. So how is it that you concluded that we now are getting into the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And once again, from the prior page, you'll see that's where the last time entries was, were 2310, 2324, and then we get to 0430 hours, so that would be the morning of the 13th then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's a wake-up call. If you go further down, then you'll see the actual times that will be 0352, 0417, 0420, so those are the reports coming in from the field. So those are the actual times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, page 28 and 29 in e-court. We see that you've concluded that this is the 13th of July and we have what -- on this 13, 7, 95, that's another Obrenovic entry in preparation?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, you'll see in the original notebook the date is written in pencil and underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now we have a new name here, Sreten Milosevic. What was -- what does this signify?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, he has written this entry. He has become the duty officer on the 13th, as he indicated to us in an interview in 2006 as well as in his testimony in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the back of this book, we'll get to it right at the end, but what information is noted in the back of the book regarding dates?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a table in the back of the book that tracks each date and who wrote each excerpt from that date, the person that was identified, and it indicates how we believe that it was that person, and as I mentioned before, that may be from a statement they made, it may be from testimony, it may be from a handwriting expert, also corroborated by reports and intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is that called the Appendix by the OTP in the back of the book?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page. Actually, I think we can just flip through those for a while because we can see that it's basically all Sreten Milosevic and a few green illegibles, and we get to 36 and 37 in e-court. And just in looking at this page, we see the portion at the top under Sreten Milosevic but was the Office of the Prosecutor able to determine, as far as you know, who wrote the bottom part of this that we don't have in red?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sreten Milosevic only identified his handwriting to the part where it says Lovac 1 and 2. We don't know who wrote the remainder of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go to 38 and 39 in e-court, the next page. And we see now Sreten Milosevic's name again with the red marks, and how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stated to us what was his handwriting in the -- in the notebook. He told us in his initial interview in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to number 40 and 41 in e-court. We have a date change, according to you. And tell us about this. Why have you concluded that we've gone now from the 13th to the 14th?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a few different reasons. One, Sretan Milosevic said he turned over the duty officer notebook or the duty to Dragan Jokic on the 14th and Dragan Jokic also confirmed in an early interview that he was the duty officer on the 14th. We also have it confirmed by our handwriting expert, Dr. Kate Barr, who conclusively confirmed that it was Dragan Jokic's handwriting. Because we know that he took over the duty on the 14th and that's his handwriting starting where you see the red notations, we have estimated that it indeed was on the 14th when he wrote this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see written in large numbering on the original Serbian, 14.07, and then it's hard to make out but you can see that Jokic has written, and again is that correct, have you double checked that, that is, as it says here, was the pencil work of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He had written that in in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, 42 and 43. And how is it that you've determined this is still the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, nothing has changed time-wise and you'll see in upcoming pages that we still are on the same date of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Dragan Jokic's entries, again, how do we know that that's Dragan Jokic for this page?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again we know that he was the duty officer as he himself told us, on the 14th, and also confirmed by Sreten Milosevic as well as Dragan Obrenovic, and also by Dr. Kate Barr when she did the handwriting analysis also concluded that it was Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, 44 and 45. You concluded that this is 14 July and we now see some times: 1000 hours, palma 1, situation battalions is regular, 1024 hours, Osmaci informed Lieutenant-Colonel Djurcic about the movements. Do these times help you determine dates at all, the actual date and time?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. As we see, it's moving along chronologically during the day, they are taking notes of what's happening throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I said, can you -- let's just skip ahead to each date change so you can give us your opinion why it is you've determined that this be the date change, and correct me if I'm wrong, but I -- I see the first date change from the 14th on at e-court 58 and 59, ERN 5753. And do you know why we see -- we see the 14/15 July up in the right, and then we see the now well-remembered italics, meaning approximately the change over. Do you know why you've concluded that this was the approximate changeover from the 14th to the 15th?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to look at the pages before this, but you'll see that the times are, once again, moving along chronologically. 2000 hours, something has been noted, something else at 2020 hours, and then the next time notated here is on this July 15th italics on the left, next to that is 0353 hours where the different battalions are reporting in on their situations, so because now it has moved to 0353 hours, we determined it was the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's jump ahead to 74 and 75 in e-court, where we see a changeover from the 15th to the 16th. And just -- Your Honours, you may recall this entry was shown to you in a prior witness, especially the notation of the Turk lawyer that escaped to Loznica hospital, wounded, treated. Sinisa. If you remember the evidence about the hospital records and Resid Sinanovic. Just to put this in context, if -- and the dates of those incidents but, again, can you tell us how is it that determined that we have a 16 July to the left here, it's not in italics?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And similar to before, the dates have been moving, the times have been moving chronologically in order. On the 15th of July throughout the day, a number of times noted: 1200 hours, 13, 14, 1500 hours, and then where you see the 16 July "I informed the IKM about that" at 0145 hours, so we've now moved into the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go ahead where it goes from 16th to the 17th, which is page 96 and 97 in e-court. Okay. And how did you determine that the changeover occurred where it's noted on the left?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, as you track the 16th of July, you'll see the times going up becoming later; 2330 hours, and then you'll see on the same page, at 2340 hours, Obrenovic reported that there is a tank, so something has been reported at 2340 hours, and then where we have notated 17 July, it's at 0005 hours, just after midnight now on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see here that the -- it's gone from Milorad Trbic to Milanko Jovicic, and I won't go into detail about that but is the evidence or information by which this was based, is that noted in the appendix at the end?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now let's jump to e-court 106 and 107, which is 5777 ERN, where we go from the 17th to the 18th, and how is it that you've determined that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way on the 17th: You'll see there is a notation at 2030 hours and then at 2100 hours, and then the next notation is at 0400 hours, from palma 2 that the situation is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go from the 18th to the 19th, which is 110 and 111 in e-court and 5779 ERN. And what do you see here that gives you an indication?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again we have been moving along on the day of the 18th, at 1554 -- 1545 hours, 1655 hours, and then where you see the 19 July just a few lines down, it says, at 0430 hours, "the enemy fired with infantry weapons." So now we've moved into the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does sometimes -- and I think you can tell from the colour version, does the handwriting and the -- and/or the colour of the inked entries change?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You'll see in the original notebook that sometimes it's blue pen or black pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that something that the investigation would consider in determining the possible change of shifts or time?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And has there been -- I think you may have mentioned this briefly, but has there been a review of the substance that is noted down in this -- in the notebook as to what may have been established by history or documentation on the same time or date?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there has been, as part of the investigation, and you'll see in the appendix, in the back, some of the supporting documents -- not all of them but some of the supporting ones that help confirm some of the events or at least who is the duty officer at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question in between?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just on this page, where you see the entry 19th of July, then right to that it is, "LPA ammunition for Praga 30 millimetres." How did you establish that this belongs to the 19th and not to the entries above related to the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, I think that actually is a very good question, because many times, as I mentioned before, the requests are often the next day, so my belief is that it may have been on the 19th earlier, the requests, but we know that for sure at 0430 hours it is the 19th. I don't know if this is a misplacement or just a general estimate of that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you look in the original? It's a little hard to tell if there is a difference in handwriting and ink colour from -- I mean it looks like there is in our colour photocopies, but maybe we could get your view on that, whether or not that is any possible indication that there is a -- a new person has come on.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in the original in this, it looks like it is the same blue ink. It's not discernable that a different pen is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The same as what? As above or below this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. All the ink on that page looks like the same blue ink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to the 19th and 20th changeover, which I have at e-court 116 and 117, and ERN 5782. And how is it that you determined that this was the changeover date?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly as you'll see in the original it's written 20 July 1995, and if you look above that boxed-in date, you'll see some times of 2210, 2239, and then immediately after the 20 July 1995 that has been written in, then you see the 0030 hours, so also helping to confirm it's the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to e-court 124 and 125. This is the changeover between the 20th and 21st of July. Again we had that italics up there next to 2400. What -- can you give us your analysis on that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the 2400 would indicate that it's midnight, and now it's on the 21st that Captain Vukotic called from the IKM. And just to confirm that, if you go down a little bit more, you see some of the early morning times, such as 0420, 0437.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And now let's get to the 22nd. E-court 136 and 137. Looks like the 21st ended on the previous page, on e-court 135, and it starts up 22nd on that page, ERN 5792. How do you determine that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as you said, the page before you see the times of 2330 hours mentioned twice, and then it jumps to 0400 hours the next day, on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go to 140 and 141, if we have a 22/23 break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in going over this, we identified that the new print-outs, the new books we made for you were missing a page here. You may not have the English translation that's up there right now. So I'm afraid we are going to have to ask you to give the books back and we'll put that in so you have a complete set. It is complete in e-court, it's just the printing missed it somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The missing page solely could be delivered to the Bench and the Defence. It's not necessary to produce a new book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I tried to figure out a way to put a page in this binding. It's a real test in fine motor skills, but we can -- yeah, we'll get that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us on this, on page e-court 141, 22/23, how you came up with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you'll see on the page before, there is quite a few times on the 22nd, starting from 0930 hours to 2137 hours, and then the next time that you see after the requests is 12 -- excuse me, 0400 hours. And you'll also see the 23 July written down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall, was there a mistake that you came across in preparing -- in one of the translations, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was numerical mistake on a time. It was written in English as 2430, when the original said 0430, and I can find the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, if you -- if that won't take you too much time. I think we can just write in the correction on the English. Sorry, I should have noted that.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you the ERN number. It's 5735.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. 5735 is --

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Number 22 and number 23. If we could put that up on e-court, e-court number 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I withdraw my proposal just to deliver a page. I realise that the last two pages have the B/C/S version on one side, and on the back side, the translation, the English translation. This is quite confusing in comparison to the whole book, only these two or three last pages have this problem. Perhaps that can be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea. A lot of effort went into this so we should get it right for the Chamber, and these are important dates so, yeah, I think that's a good idea. And we'll also correct this error as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you point out to us where this error is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right at the bottom. The last time that you see is 2430.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what should that be, according to the original?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, and if you look to the left side it's clearly a 0. It should be 0430.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to finish up, let's -- where you go from 23 to 24, it's e-court 144 and 145. How do you come up with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And once again the page before, you'll see the times going up to 2025. And then underneath where you see Strbac, the wake-up at 0430 hours, you then see it says -- it says 00 hours palma 2 reported that the 4th and 7th infantry battalions have been provoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I -- that's the last -- pretty much the last section that this exhibit has used, and then after that we have the appendix, which you've already spoke of, so on -- that's fundamentally all my questions, Mr. President and Your Honours, and we will provide everyone with a better book, and of course General Tolimir will be able to cross-examine at a later date, when I speak with Mr. Gajic and they are ready to do that. We'll also -- we are also in the process of identifying for all of us where we are with Dusan Janc, Mr. Blaszczyk, and Ms. Gallagher so we are all clear on that. I'm not exactly clear myself. But in any event, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you shouldn't produce a whole new book. We should -- we shouldn't waste paper and woods. We should save some woods, especially after the conference in Mexico, and therefore I am inclined to give it back to you so that only the last pages should be changed, and then perhaps after the recess, we can get the new one in the right order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll try to do that, and I'm not sure if we need to print out a few new pages or not. Somehow I got one that didn't have those problems but we'll get on that before we forget what this book is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be able to check that with your team. Is there anything else to raise for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could offer into evidence now or we could wait until cross-examination, but I would like this to be part of the evidence, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is again which 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this is 65 ter 361A, which is based on the original 65 ter number of the book that it comes from, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P14, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any objection. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I see in my e-court that this has already been tendered as P5361A. No, no. I'm sorry, I apologise. I'm seeing something else. I'm sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. This document -- Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So that Ms. Gallagher doesn't have to wait, can we put some questions right now that the Defence can put to her and then we can resolve this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. First we should receive this book with 65 ter number 361A as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document shall be given Exhibit P01459. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. By the agreement that we had, this was going to be direct only but there is only ten minutes left, I'm sure Ms. Gallagher can take on some questions, though it was her understanding from me that this would be direct only, so -- and she has endeavoured to come up to speed, as you can see, but I think a few questions by the general shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think so too. And after the recess, the witness will not be prepared in a better way than today because she will not be allowed to discuss with you during the break about the content of her testimony. Mr. Tolimir, you may commence your cross-examination, just start with it for the last ten minutes of today's hearing. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet Ms. Gallagher who joined us late. I'm not going to be putting too many questions to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question that I put during the cross-examination already is already familiar to you. I would like to repeat it: Was it possible for somebody to take this notebook and to enter additional data about the time, the persons, about themselves, about activities, and did the Prosecution establish if there were some cases like that in relation to the critical dates?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the dates that a witness, a duty officer, has confirmed that it is his handwriting, that certainly hasn't been an issue. They have confirmed that everything that is in their portion is their own handwriting and that no one else has tampered with it or added anything to it. And that also is confirmed by the handwriting expert when she has looked at the portions written by, for example, Dragan Jokic, or Drago Nikolic and various people. That's part of their expertise is determining that it's not written by any other people, so in the sections that we've determined to be written by a person, that's -- would not be possible. In the other sections, where we don't know who has written, I guess theoretically that's always a possibility. You'll see as you look at the notebook, however, that you don't see that there are pages torn out, you don't see things that are crossed out or whited out. You'll see that things are spaced as though they were writing contemporaneously throughout the notebook. And if I can add, that it has been a notebook that has been used not only by the witnesses themselves who wrote in the book but many other people from the Zvornik Brigade, commanders on down, who have relied upon the book for its accuracy, and at no time has it been determined that the book has been tampered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you if the OTP established if anything was added later. Perhaps you can just help me with this so that I can use the ten minutes that I was granted by His Honour the Presiding Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that the OTP has determined that has been added later has been the parts in pencil. It's been the dates in pencil and a couple of the notations of the duty officer that Dragan Obrenovic had stated to us that he had added in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you on page 6924 who changed the date of the 12th of July, and you replied, on page 70, that this was changed and estimated -- and the change was estimated to be on the basis of a change. This is ERN number 0293-5731. If it's hard to find your way around, perhaps everybody can look in the e-court. That will be easier for everybody. If you can look at pages 12, 13 in the e-court, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those, the ERN pages would be 14 and 15 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you kindly show pages 12 and 13 in the e-court because it will be obvious to all of us who are looking at that. In a short time I will show what I would like to show. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: However, this is a different ERN number than you indicated earlier. But it's on the screen now. You may put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I mentioned the number deliberately because it's difficult to see the difference in the dates on page 530 that we are looking at now -- actually, 730, we can see the first entry, and underneath that we can see that it says "Order" using the same ink, and then we see what the measures are that are ordered. But then if we look at the contents, Ms. Gallagher, of this first thing at 1910 hours, it says, "Enemy radio activated," and so on and so forth. And then there is an order that follows: "Take all measures of combat security." And then in the same ink, it says: "Absence of the commander is still not permitted." This entry was made, according to this, before the 12th, allegedly, it was entered on the 11th and you can see the time, 19:19:19, and then later you can see 330 under those two paragraphs, and then at the bottom you can see the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Ms. Gallagher, why is the break between this information about enemy activity and the order that relates to the same event, to the same ink, and to the same person, and it was written at such and such a time but it was transferred to this other side where it says 1900 hours? I'm sorry, actually it's not 1200 hours, it says the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The short question is: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. As I mentioned before, I am assuming that it was determined that the -- that it became the 12th of July at the point of these orders only because it has been the pattern that the orders and requests have happened later in the evening, past midnight, sometime before usually 5.00 in the morning. I do think, however, it's -- it would not be inappropriate to also have it down closer to the 0345 hours, but I think that is why it was determined that it was on -- that the time had already moved into the 12th of July because of the pattern of when orders have usually been issued, and the requests as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gallagher. This information that is written at the beginning where enemy activity is discussed require the urgent issuance of measures by the person who received it, or is it necessary to wait a whole night before anything can happen? Wouldn't it be more logical that the same person noted this down at the same time because it was a matter of urgency? And it's the same handwriting, the dates are not different.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do agree with you; I think that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: Were all the entries authorised by the duty officers for the critical dates? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I can ask, what do you mean by "authorised by the duty officers"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It means that they signed it, that they handed over their duty that day and that they verified that they made the entries on that day so that they would not be ascribed to someone else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- as you see from the duty officer notebook that they are not signing in that, so it's not being authorised in the notebook itself with their signatures or the time that they turned it over. We have relied upon their statements and testimony, usually, for when they have turned the duty over to the next duty officer or to an assistant duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. The last one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I just wanted to ask Ms. Gallagher if she knew if any handwriting analysis was done on the parts of the handwritings for the critical dates, for the critical times, and for the critical entries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be a bit subjective as to which are the critical dates and times and entries but certainly you'll see from the notebook and from the -- from Dr. Kate Barr's reports that many of the key dates of times or dates when we didn't know who the duty officer was or were unsure or wanted that confirmation, those dates and those -- that handwriting was analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer with a yes or a no because we are out of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the handwriting -- it's a difficult "yes" or "no" question. The handwriting analysis was done on those critical dates and times where the duty officer -- where we didn't know or were not sure who the -- who had written it. Where we did know who had written it, then the handwriting analysis was not necessary because they told us that they -- they identified it as their own handwriting, so it's both yes and no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think now is an appropriate time to adjourn. You have put the first questions to the witness in cross-examination and sometime next year it should be continued and the parties will agree on the appropriate time. We adjourn, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There is no need. We have finished our cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, Ms. Gallagher, you are free to return to your normal activities, work for the OTP, and I wish you a good break time during Christmas and New Year's Eve. You are free now to leave the courtroom. We all do that now, we adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of December 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
